title: How to Compare Upfront Dental Prices Across Clinics
description: A checklist for getting comparable written prices from several dental offices without joining a plan, and for spotting the quote that is hiding a stage.
main_html:
Quick answer

You can get comparable dental prices without joining a plan. You have to ask every office the same question, in the same words, and get the answer in writing.

The reason this works is that dental quotes vary far more by scope than by price. Two offices quoting the same procedure are often quoting different amounts of work.

The five-question script

Use this on the phone, then ask for it by email. The written version is the one that matters.

  1. What are the CDT codes for the treatment you are recommending?
  2. What is the self-pay price for each code, before any insurance?
  3. Which items are excluded from that total and billed separately?
  4. What could change the plan after imaging, and by roughly how much?
  5. Is there a fee for the consultation or the imaging if I do not proceed?

An office that answers all five in writing has told you a great deal about how it will behave later.

Why "average cost" pages cannot help you here

The ADA discontinued its Survey of Dental Fees in 2023 and is barred by federal law from quoting or recommending fees.

Medicare does not cover routine restorative dentistry, so no federal price data exists for crowns, bridges or standard implants either.

That leaves the written quote as the only real number in this market. Collecting three of them beats reading any national average.

When this checklist matters most

Large treatment plans. Anything staged across several visits. Any conversation where financing arrives before the diagnosis does.

It matters less for a single filling, where scope is unlikely to shift underneath you.

Questions to ask about the plan itself

  • Which items are urgent, and which could wait six months?
  • What is the cheaper option you did not recommend, and why not?
  • Who performs the work, and is a specialist referral likely?
  • What is the policy if the work needs redoing?

Red flags

Refusal to put codes in writing. A quote that expires today. Pressure that increases the moment you mention budget.

Common mistake: accepting a verbal number and discovering the crown was quoted separately.

What a usable written estimate actually contains

A verbal figure is not an estimate, and a single total is barely one. What makes an estimate usable is that each item on it is named separately, so you can see what you are being charged for and so a second office can quote the same list. Ask for it itemised, ask for it before any work begins, and ask for it to be dated, because fee schedules change.

  • Each procedure listed as its own line, with the tooth or teeth it applies to.
  • The procedure code for each line, which is what lets your insurer and any other office identify precisely the same treatment.
  • Which lines are diagnostic, which are the treatment, and which are follow-up or review.
  • What the estimate assumes about your insurance, and what the figure becomes if that assumption is wrong.
  • A clear statement of what is excluded, and how long the estimate stands.

Keep the copy. If a later invoice differs, the dated itemised estimate is the only basis on which that conversation can be had calmly. An office that is reluctant to produce one is telling you something useful at no cost to you.

The scope-change conversation, agreed in advance

Most dental bills that end in a dispute did not involve overcharging. They involved a plan that changed once treatment started and a patient who was never asked. Dentistry genuinely does reveal more once a filling is out or an image is read, so scope change is normal. What should not be normal is finding out at the desk.

Settle the rule beforehand. Ask what the office does when it finds something unplanned mid-procedure: stops and discusses, proceeds and informs you afterwards, or proceeds only up to an agreed figure. Ask whether you can set a threshold above which nothing is added without your explicit agreement, and ask for that to be noted on the plan. Ask who is authorised to agree additional work if you are sedated and cannot.

Ask also what happens in the other direction. If planned work turns out not to be needed, is the estimate reduced? The answer is usually yes, and asking the question signals that you are reading the plan as a two-way document rather than a bill in waiting.

Staging, priority, and what can safely wait

A long treatment plan presented as a single total is the hardest thing to say yes to and the easiest thing to walk away from entirely, which serves nobody. Nearly every plan can be sequenced, and sequencing it is a clinical question rather than a financial one: some work is urgent, some prevents deterioration, and some is elective and can sit for a year without harm.

Ask the office to sort the plan into what needs doing now, what should be done within months, and what is genuinely elective. Ask what the consequence of delay is for each item, specifically, because "it will get worse" is not a timeline. Ask whether staging changes the total, since some work is cheaper done together and some is not.

Then ask what the plan would be if only the urgent part were done. A practice that can answer that without making you feel awkward is one that will treat you honestly for years. A practice that treats the full plan as all-or-nothing has turned a clinical recommendation into a sales position, and that is worth noticing before you commit to the first appointment rather than after.

What to do next

Call three offices with the same script. Put the three written estimates next to each other and compare code by code.

If the totals differ by more than a third, the scopes almost certainly differ too. Find out where before you decide.
